html:
The world is grappling with a significant escalation in the Houthi conflict with Saudi Arabia, following deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s international airport and another facility, killing at least 13 people and injuring hundreds. The Houthi attacks have prompted Saudi Arabia to vow a "serious response" and led to international outcry, with President Donald Trump stating the attacks were "not acceptable" and his administration weighing potential US strikes against the Houthis and Iran.

Regional Security: Amidst the heightened tensions, Iran has offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia, while simultaneously expressing deep concern over the escalation, which it claims benefits "only" Israel. The Iranian IRGC Navy also announced that a supertanker exploded and a third oil tanker caught fire after striking sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran's military leaders threatening to target cables, data centers, and AI facilities if fighting resumes. Riyadh airport has suspended operations, with some reports indicating it will remain closed until October 17, and Houthi forces have warned airlines against using Saudi airspace.

Great Power Politics: Conflicting reports have emerged regarding the Russia-Ukraine conflict, following President Donald Trump’s declaration of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the agreement was "news to me" and Russia had already violated it with attacks on energy sites. The Kremlin, for its part, rejected a 60-day truce offer and refused to comment on Trump's declaration. Meanwhile, Ukraine continues its strikes on Russian data centers, and NATO’s Top Commander outlined plans to thwart a potential Russian attack on the Alliance.

UK Politics: In the United Kingdom, prime minister Andy Burnham reopened the debate over Russia's alleged interference in the 2016 Brexit referendum, though No 10 reiterated that Burnham accepts the result as "legitimate." Separately, Nigel Farage’s party, Reform UK, unveiled hardline immigration policies, proposing the immediate deportation of 90,000 asylum seekers, including children and mothers, and a five-year ban on asylum grants.

Global Economy: US economists Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were awarded the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work on models that help central bankers and finance ministers stabilize economies. In the automotive sector, Chinese car brands are posing steep competition to Western carmakers at the Paris Motor Show, indicating a shift in global market dynamics. Reports also suggest that aides to Roman Abramovich falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, with Deloitte allegedly assisting in hiding billions. Separately, Norway's sovereign wealth fund is withdrawing investments from Israeli banks, citing concerns over "genocide" in Gaza and crimes in the West Bank.

US Developments: Federal agents searched the home of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation, following accusations of immigration fraud by President Donald Trump and his allies. The US also detained Álvaro Pulido, a man accused in a multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme, for whom officials had offered a $10 million reward. The Justice Department has also launched an antitrust probe into several TV networks.

Other Global Events: Indian opposition leaders led a march to the top court in Delhi to demand the election chief resign, after thousands of protesters were detained over the weekend. Elsewhere, Pope Leo XIV announced he would undergo lung surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule." In France, a fire devastated Le Marché des Enfants Rouges, Paris's oldest covered food market, and a 14-year-old pupil was arrested after two teachers were shot at a French school. The European Union also warned digital platforms against livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, scheduled for December 3.
